name: High-protein diet

card.summary: Protein-forward eating for muscle retention and fullness; supported for those goals, untested for hair or skin claims.
card.note: Kidney effects at very high intakes are debated; people with kidney disease are advised to consult clinicians.

quick.overview:
A high-protein diet raises protein above the standard 0.8 g/kg recommended allowance, usually through meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. It is popular for cutting and muscle building.

Higher intake is linked to more muscle and less muscle loss during energy deficits; claims about hair or skin have not been tested.
quick.mechanism: Protein increases satiety, has a higher thermic effect than carbohydrates or fat, and supplies amino acids for muscle repair.
quick.risks: Reviews disagree on kidney risk at higher intakes. Restrictive versions may cause constipation, headaches or bad breath, and the AHA has cautioned about diets high in saturated fat.

lead: A high-protein diet builds meals around protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes and protein powders. People use it to look leaner and more muscular: protein supplies the amino acids for muscle repair after training, helps preserve lean mass while calories are cut, and tends to keep people fuller, so a lean physique is easier to maintain. Wikipedia notes that such diets are commonly used for fat loss and muscle building.[1]

Definitions vary. Wikipedia describes a high-protein diet as one drawing 40 percent or more of daily calories from protein, while sports-nutrition sources count anything above the US recommended dietary allowance of 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, with typical ranges of about 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg for active people.[1][2][18] The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) gives 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg per day as sufficient for most exercisers to build or maintain muscle.[11]

The idea has two lineages: the commercial diet books of the 1970s onward, such as Atkins and Dukan, which paired high protein with low carbohydrate and were sold for weight loss, and the bodybuilding and strength-training tradition, in which protein targets are set to maximise muscle. In looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is discussed mainly for physique, and in some posts for hair, skin and other tissues; a social-media trend called protein maxxing centres on maximising daily intake.[2][14] Research links higher protein intake with greater muscle mass and less muscle loss in an energy deficit, while reviews disagree about long-term kidney and cardiovascular effects.[1][13][15]

chain: Higher protein intake supplies amino acids for muscle repair
Combined with resistance training, supports muscle gain and preserves lean mass in a calorie deficit
Greater satiety and thermic effect make leanness easier to maintain
angle.text: Protein works through training and calorie control: it supports muscle growth after lifting and helps hold on to lean tissue while fat is lost, which shapes the visible physique. Claims that very high intake improves hair or skin are discussed in forums but have not been tested in trials.

paras: Wikipedia lists foods typical of the pattern as lean beef, poultry, pork, salmon, tuna, eggs, dairy and soy. Many commercial high-protein diets also restrict carbohydrates, and some are high in saturated fat.[1] Named examples include Atkins, Dukan, Montignac, Protein Power, Scarsdale, Stillman, Sugar Busters!, the Zone and the protein-sparing modified fast.[1]

A proposed classification in the sports-nutrition literature labels intakes below 1.25 g/kg per day as low, 1.25 to 1.9 as moderate, 1.9 to 3.4 as high and above 3.4 as very high; its authors note average intake is about 1.3 g/kg and that conventional high-protein diets run about 1.8 to 3 g/kg.[4]

Protein is built from amino acids; nine are essential and cannot be made by the body, and protein quality is scored by methods such as PDCAAS, adopted by the FDA and FAO/WHO in 1993, and DIAAS, proposed by the FAO in 2013.[18] The US and Canadian Dietary Reference Intakes give 46 g per day for women and 56 g for men aged 19 to 70, based on 0.8 g/kg, and Wikipedia notes that this figure covers structural needs only.[18] Average US intake in NHANES 2013-2014 was about 70 g for women and 98 g for men.[18]

Lifters use higher protein intakes to support muscle hypertrophy, and people cutting body fat use them to retain muscle while losing weight. Higher intake is associated with greater muscle mass, better adaptation to resistance training and less muscle loss during energy deficit, according to Wikipedia.[1] Protein raises satiety through gut hormones such as GLP-1, CCK and PYY, and carries a larger thermic cost of digestion than carbohydrate or fat, according to a review of the clinical evidence.[21]

Wikipedia's article on protein reports that strength athletes may need 1.4 to 1.8 g/kg per day, endurance athletes 1.2 to 1.4 g/kg, and athletes restricting calories 1.8 to 2.0 g/kg.[18] On the T Nation forum, protein-heavy plans such as the Velocity Diet, a shake-based fat-loss programme, have been discussed and revisited for years by members who describe feeling full on high protein intake.[8]

High-protein, low-calorie diets are often used in obesity treatment.[1] A 2022 commentary in Nature Metabolism discussed a high-protein diet in relation to preventing weight regain.[10] People with chronic kidney disease are the reverse case: Wikipedia reports that those who reduce protein to 0.6 to 0.8 g/kg per day have less risk of progressing to end-stage kidney disease.[18]

Wikipedia traces the best-known commercial form to cardiologist Robert Atkins, who published Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution in 1972, drawing on earlier low-carbohydrate work by Alfred Pennington. The diet peaked in 2003 and 2004, when about one in eleven North American adults said they followed a low-carb plan, and Atkins Nutritionals filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July 2005 after demand fell.[16] The article also records criticism that Atkins did not publish clinical data on his patients and the statements of the American Heart Association, American Medical Association and American Dietetic Association calling the diet nutritionally unbalanced.[16]

Pierre Dukan, a Paris general practitioner, began developing his four-phase high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet in 1975, and published it in 2000 in the book Je ne sais pas maigrir, which Wikipedia reports has sold more than 7 million copies. It reached the UK in 2010 and the US in 2011. Wikipedia notes that the British Dietetic Association listed it as a top diet to avoid, and that Dukan was barred from practising as a GP for eight days in 2013 over a diet pill he prescribed in the 1970s.[17]

The bodybuilding tradition runs separately. Shake-based plans such as the Velocity Diet circulated on T Nation, where members were still writing about it 15 years later.[8] In sports nutrition, the ISSN issued a position stand on protein and exercise in 2017.[11] Government guidance has shifted too: Wikipedia reports that the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, released in January 2026 under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., prioritise protein and encourage meat and dairy, while Stanford's Nutrition Studies Research Group praised parts of the document and criticised the protein emphasis.[19]

A 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine pooled 49 randomised trials with 1,863 participants and found that protein supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training increased fat-free mass by about 0.3 kg and strength by about 2.5 kg on average. Gains in fat-free mass shrank with age and were larger in resistance-trained people, and total intake above about 1.62 g/kg per day produced no further training-related gains.[15]

A 2005 trial reported that a high-protein diet sustained reductions in appetite, calorie intake and body weight despite compensatory changes in leptin and ghrelin.[3] A 2010 trial in the New England Journal of Medicine examined diets with high or low protein content and glycemic index for weight-loss maintenance in overweight adults from eight European countries.[5] A review of clinical trials reports that, above the RDA, protein reduced body weight and fat mass while preserving fat-free mass in both low-calorie and standard-calorie diets, with trials of 6 to 12 months showing weight-loss effects and less regain.[21]
Grokipedia summarises trials as showing about 0.79 kg more weight loss with higher-protein diets than standard-protein diets and up to 0.43 kg more fat-free mass retained over 6 to 12 months.[2]

The ISSN position stand describes distributing protein across the day in doses of about 0.25 g/kg or 20 to 40 g, roughly every 3 to 4 hours, with total daily intake mattering more than precise timing and timing benefits shrinking when intake is already around 1.6 g/kg or higher. It reports that whey is the most studied fast-digesting source, casein is used before sleep, and that milk, eggs and beef are high-quality sources, while soy ranks lower in essential-amino-acid and leucine content.[11]

For resistance-trained people in a calorie deficit, the ISSN position stand reports that intakes of 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg per day may help retain lean mass.[11] A 2023 trial in young adults compared vegan and omnivorous high-protein diets and examined muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy.[12]

On looksmax.org, one poster asked whether "mass amounts" of protein could support hair, collagen, the nervous system and bones, and a reply suggested little marginal benefit past about 1 g per pound.[14] T Nation also hosts a long-running thread asking how much protein is needed for muscle growth.[20]

A 2005 trial measured appetite, ad libitum calorie intake and body weight on a high-protein diet.[3] A 2010 multicentre trial examined protein and glycemic index in weight-loss maintenance.[5] A 2013 meta-analysis compared dietary approaches for type 2 diabetes,[6] and Wikipedia reports a 2020 meta-analysis that found no significant improvement in blood pressure or glycemic control among people with type 2 diabetes.[1]

A 2017 randomized trial in 100 overweight and obese adults aged 55 to 80 used a 2x2 design over a 10-week weight-loss programme to test whether a high-protein diet and or resistance exercise preserved fat-free mass.[7] A 12-week randomized trial in 55 postmenopausal women examined resistance training combined with a high-protein diet on body composition, muscle thickness and strength.[9] A 2023 trial in young adults compared vegan and omnivorous high-protein diets for muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy.[12]

A 2023 commentary and systematic review examined testosterone: a prior meta-analysis had found very high protein intakes above 3.4 g/kg per day lowered men's total testosterone, and the commentary concluded that moderate and high intakes of 1.25 to 3.4 g/kg did not.[4] No controlled trials were found that test high protein intake for hair, skin or facial appearance.

A 2017 review suggested intake above 1.5 g/kg of ideal body weight may contribute to kidney damage, whereas a 2023 umbrella review found no evidence that intake above 0.8 g/kg/day specifically triggers chronic kidney disease.[1] A 2020 review in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology described how high protein can raise glomerular pressure and kidney hyperfiltration and noted observational links between animal protein and end-stage kidney disease, while stating that confounding and conflicting trial results mean long-term studies are needed.[13] A review of clinical evidence reports that high-protein diets have not been shown to harm bone density or renal function in healthy adults.[21] Wikipedia's article on protein notes that no tolerable upper intake level has been set, that excess intake may raise urinary calcium and kidney stone risk, and that a meta-analysis found no adverse effect on bone density.[18]

The American Heart Association has said diets high in protein and saturated fat raise the risk of coronary artery disease and cancer, and its 2001 committee advised against some high-protein diets citing a lack of long-term studies.[1] Wikipedia also cites a 2014 review linking fad diets to urinary stone formation.[1][17] Reported effects of restrictive versions include constipation, headaches and bad breath, particularly with low fibre intake, and people with kidney, liver or diabetic conditions are advised to consult clinicians.[2]

Protein-focused eating has moved from the diet-book era of Atkins in the 1970s to fitness forums and short-video trends such as protein maxxing, in which users aim to maximise daily protein intake.[2] Commercial plans such as the Velocity Diet have been discussed for years on bodybuilding forums.[8] Wikipedia's account of the 2025-2030 US guidelines shows protein becoming a topic of public-health politics, including a Super Bowl LX advertisement on 8 February 2026 featuring Mike Tyson that promoted avoiding processed foods.[19]

Wikipedia notes that critics of the commercial diets say they promote misconceptions about carbohydrates, insulin resistance and ketosis, and that researchers disagree about how well and how safely they work.[1] Wikipedia's Atkins article records a 2004 lawsuit over cholesterol that was dismissed in 2007 and a 2021 review describing the diet as returning to the quackery scene.[16]

lore.intro: Forum users debate how much protein is useful beyond muscle building, from kidney concerns to claims about hair, skin and collagen.[14][20]

claims.claim: Very high protein intake improves hair, skin, collagen and other tissues beyond muscle.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster asked whether mass amounts of protein could support hair, collagen, the nervous system and bones depleted by lifting, while replies suggested little marginal benefit beyond about 1 g per pound.[14]
claims.experts: No published trials were found testing very high protein intake for hair, skin or facial appearance; kidney effects at high intakes are debated.[1][13]

claims.claim: Protein-heavy plans such as the Velocity Diet help people get lean quickly.
claims.believers: T Nation members have written logs and reviews of shake-based high-protein plans and describe feeling full and satiated on them.[8]
claims.experts: Trials show modestly greater weight loss and fat-free mass retention with higher protein intake than with standard protein, while the American Heart Association has cautioned about high-protein diets that are also high in saturated fat.[1][2][21]

claims.claim: More protein always builds more muscle.
claims.believers: Many lifters set targets well above the RDA and some go to 1 g per pound of bodyweight or more.[14][20]
claims.experts: A 2018 meta-analysis found no further training-related gains in fat-free mass above about 1.62 g/kg per day, while the ISSN says 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg suffices for most exercisers and that higher intakes may help retain lean mass in a deficit.[11][15]

claims.claim: High protein intake damages healthy kidneys.
claims.believers: Posters sometimes preface questions with "kidney failure aside", reflecting a common concern in lifting communities.[14]
claims.experts: A 2020 nephrology review says long-term high protein may raise hyperfiltration and possibly cause de novo kidney disease but that long-term studies are needed; a 2023 umbrella review found no evidence that intake above 0.8 g/kg specifically triggers CKD.[1][13]

claims.claim: Very high protein intake lowers testosterone.
claims.believers: The claim circulated after a 2022 meta-analysis of low-carbohydrate diets in men.[4]
claims.experts: A 2023 analysis reports that only very high intakes above 3.4 g/kg per day appeared to lower testosterone, whereas intakes of 1.25 to 3.4 g/kg did not.[4]

claims.claim: Plant-based protein cannot support muscle growth as well as animal protein.
claims.believers: Lifting communities have long favoured whey, eggs and beef as protein sources.[11]
claims.experts: A 2023 trial in young adults compared vegan and omnivorous high-protein diets for muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy, and its title reports comparable rates; the ISSN notes soy ranks lower in leucine content.[11][12]
